paragraphs: §1 — Each person is arraigned over every single one of his acts; the order of the classes brought to judgment

We say that the disobedient, at the time of the resurrection (al-maʿād), must inevitably be arraigned (yuwāqaf) over each and every single one of all that he did and committed. The proof of that is the saying of [Amos, peace be upon him,] [Amos 4:13] כִּי הִנֵּה יוֹצֵר הָרִים וּבוֹרֵא רוּחַ וּמַגִּיד לְאָדָם מַה שֵּׂחוֹ ("for behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought") etc. — for he reported that He informs the human being of all that he uttered and said; yet we have not seen Him inform people of that in this world, so we knew that He informs them of it only in the world to come; and that is His arraigning them over what they did, one thing at a time. And that too is the meaning of the saying [Jer 23:24] אִם יִסָּתֵר אִישׁ בַּמִּסְתָּרִים וַאֲנִי לֹא אֶרְאֶנּוּ נְאֻם יְיָ ("if a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him? says the Lord") etc., and His saying at the end of the account [Ps 50:21] גַּם כֹּה אֹכִיחֲךָ וְאֶעֶרְכָה לְעֵינֶיךָ ("I will reprove you, and set [the matter] in order before your eyes"). And this saying refers to the judgment (ḥukm) of the world to come, since he says at the beginning of the passage [Ps 50:1] אֵל אֱלֹהִים יְיָ דִּבֶּר וַיִּקְרָא אָרֶץ ("God, the Lord God, has spoken and summoned the earth") etc. — and that is the Day of Judgment; and he said [Ps 50:3] כִּי יָבוֹא אֱלֹהֵינוּ וְאַל יֶחֱרַשׁ ("our God comes and shall not keep silent"), meaning He does not refrain from the litigation (al-muḥākama) and the calling to account (al-muṭālaba); then he said [Ps 50:4] יִקְרָא אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם מֵעָל וְאֶל הָאָרֶץ ("He summons the heavens above, and the earth") etc. — so he made it known that this saying refers to the Day of Judgment. Then he said [Ps 50:5] אִסְפוּ לִי חֲסִידָי כֹּרְתֵי בְרִיתִי עֲלֵי זָבַח ("gather to Me My faithful, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice") — so he made known by that that the first to be brought forward for judgment are the choicest and the righteous (al-akhyār wa-l-ṣulaḥāʾ); then, after them, the middling ones (al-awsāṭ), who are the generality, on account of his saying [Ps 50:7] שִׁמְעָה עַמִּי וַאֲדַבֵּר ("hear, My people, and I will speak") etc., [and] לֹא עַל זְבָחֶיךָ אוֹכִיחֶךָ ("not for your sacrifices do I reprove you") etc.; and after the middling ones, the wicked (al-fussāq), on account of his saying [Ps 50:16] וְלָרָשָׁע אָמַר אֱלֹהִים מַה לְּךָ ("but to the wicked God says: what have you to do [to declare My statutes]") etc. — so he reported that He enumerates his acts one thing at a time, as has been mentioned and described. And among the proofs also for the arraignment over each single thing is his saying [Joel 4:2] וְקִבַּצְתִּי אֶת כָּל הַגּוֹיִם וְהוֹרַדְתִּים ("and I will gather all the nations and bring them down") etc. — for he reported that He arraigns [each one] over each single thing.

: The opening establishes the muwāqafa (arraignment): in the eschaton the disobedient is confronted item-by-item with every deed. Muwāqafa / yuwāqaf (the staged glossary §VI anchor-term muwāqafa) is Q's technical name for the eschatological interrogation that "some people call al-ḥisāb" (the reckoning) — the heading's careful "some people call" distancing suggests ḥisāb is the popular (perhaps Rabbanite or Muslim-colored) name for what Q prefers to call arraignment. The prooftext chain is exegetically tight: Amos 4:13 (God "declares to man his thought") cannot refer to this world, since no such declaration is observed here, so it must be the next; Jer 23:24 and the Psalm-50 theophany supply the courtroom imagery. The graded order of judgment — akhyār/ṣulaḥāʾ (righteous) → awsāṭ (the middling majority) → fussāq (the wicked) — is read straight out of the sequence of addressees in Ps 50 (vv. 5, 7, 16): the manzila bayna al-manzilatayn (the intermediate station) of Bahshamī moral theology mapped onto the Psalm's three audiences.
§2 — Each class beholds the lot of the other; this is known both from Scripture and from reason

And among the proofs that each one of the people of reward and the people of punishment beholds the [state of] every group that is in the other class is His saying [Mal 3:18] וְשַׁבְתֶּם וּרְאִיתֶם בֵּין צַדִּיק לְרָשָׁע ("and you shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked"), and also His saying [Isa 66:24] וְיָצְאוּ וְרָאוּ בְּפִגְרֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים ("and they shall go forth and look upon the corpses of the men [who rebelled against Me]"). And this may also be known by reason (ʿaqlan): namely that the soul is so disposed by nature (maṭbūʿa) as to gladness and joy when it beholds affliction upon its enemy, and to grief and sorrow when it beholds him in bliss and felicity. So one who is in the [state of] reward and beholds his enemy in affliction and punishment — his joy is thereby increased in his reward and his beatitude; and that is the meaning of his saying [Mic 7:10] וְתֵרֶא אֹיַבְתִּי וּתְכַסֶּהָ בוּשָׁה ("my enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her"), and his saying [Mic 7:10] עֵינַי תִּרְאֶינָה בָּהּ ("my eyes shall gaze upon her") etc. And likewise one who is in [the state of] punishment and beholds his enemy and adversary in bliss — his sorrow and grief thereby are increased in his pain and his punishment; and that too is the meaning of his saying [Ezek 28:26] וְיָשְׁבוּ עָלֶיהָ לָבֶטַח ("and they shall dwell upon it securely") etc., and his saying [Ps 92:12] וּבְקָמִים עָלַי מְרֵעִים ("upon the evildoers who rise against me [my eyes have looked]"), and his saying [Prov 24:17-18] יִרְאוּ גוֹיִם וְיֵבֹשׁוּ ("the nations shall see and be ashamed") etc.
: The source has al-ghamm wa-l-ḥuzn (grief and sorrow); rendered as a hendiadys.

: For the citation cluster of §2 the OCR is heavily corrupted (the diff-report logs 77 Hebrew disagreements across these pages); the verse references in brackets are reconstructed from the legible fragments against the Masoretic text. Two of Q's marginal pointers are partly illegible: the כְּשֵׂם … שֶׁבֶּן הָאִישׁ הַטּוֹב לִבְּכֶם fragment that precedes the Micah citation in the source resists secure identification and is omitted rather than invented (see translator's notes); the וְיָשְׁבוּ עָלֶיהָ לָבֶטַח pointer reads bi-Yeḥezqe[l] [kaf-ḥet, kaf-waw] = Ezek 28:26.

: Q's second eschatological thesis: each class sees the other's lot — Mal 3:18 and Isa 66:24 supplying the scriptural warrant. The remarkable move is the rational supplement (ʿaqlan): the soul is "disposed by nature" (maṭbūʿa) to take satisfaction in an enemy's affliction and grief at an enemy's good fortune — so the mutual beholding is not arbitrary but augments reward (the blessed see their foes punished) and aggravates punishment (the damned see their foes blessed). This Schadenfreude-as-recompense psychology is a naturalizing, kalām-style grounding of an eschatological datum; the prophetic verses (Mic 7:10; Ezek 28:26; Ps 92:12; Prov 24:17-18) are read as describing precisely this asymmetric seeing.
§3 — Retribution for the wronged from the wrongdoer; the view of "some" that merits and demerits are transferred

And among the proofs for the taking of retribution (al-qiṣāṣ) for the wronged from the wrongdoer is his saying [Ezek 34:17, 20] הִנְנִי שׁוֹפֵט בֵּין שֶׂה בִרְיָה וּבֵין שֶׂה רָזָה ("behold, I will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep") — meaning the wrongdoer, who grew fat upon the property of the wronged and left him lean: it is taken from him [in retribution] for [the wronged]. And likewise also the like of his saying [Ezek 39:10] וְשָׁלְלוּ אֶת שֹׁלְלֵיהֶם וּבָזְזוּ אֶת בֹּזְזֵיהֶם ("and they shall despoil those who despoiled them, and plunder those who plundered them") etc.

Now if someone says: "this is admissible only in this world, in which a human being has property and possession that can be taken from him by virtue of the king who owns it; but in the world to come, what is there to be taken from him and recovered, so that it might be returned to the wronged?" — we say: some have stated, on this question, a doctrine that is not far-fetched; rather analogy (al-qiyās) would require it. It is that whoever wronged a man in this world has [some] of the wrongdoer's good deeds (ḥasanāt) taken from him in the world to come and handed over to the wronged; and if the wrongdoer have no good deeds, [some] of the wronged man's evil deeds (sayyiʾāt) are taken and cast upon the wrongdoer — since the Creator (sublime and mighty be He) is just (ʿadlan), and the retribution must inevitably take place, as the foregoing statement has it.

: The retribution thesis: Q grounds eschatological qiṣāṣ in the prophetic pastoral imagery (Ezek 34's fat-vs-lean sheep = oppressor fattened on the victim's substance; Ezek 39:10's despoiling of the despoilers). The objection is sharp and material: retribution in this world works by transferring confiscable property under a king's coercive power — but the next world has no property to seize. The reported answer ("some have said … and qiyās would require it") is the transfer-of-deeds doctrine: the oppressor's ḥasanāt (merits) pass to the victim, or, failing those, the victim's sayyiʾāt (demerits) pass to the oppressor. This is the well-known iḥbāṭ wa-takfīr economy of Bahshamī moral bookkeeping (staged glossary §VI: iḥbāṭ, takfīr), here applied to interpersonal wrong. Q reports it at one remove ("some have said") and grounds it in divine justice (ʿadl) — note he does not yet endorse it; §4 will give what "is sound in our view."
§4 — Q's own preferred view: restitution of double, on the model of the law of theft and bodily injury

But what is sound in our view is this doctrine: that the Creator (exalted be He) made it obligatory upon the thief and the wrongdoer to return to the wronged twice over (ḍiʿfay) what the wrongdoer and the thief took from him; and that if he is not able to do that, he is enslaved [in payment]. For if one who was wronged, and from whom the right was not exacted in this world, were to incur only [his oppressor's] punishment in the world to come, without anything returning to the wronged, then his case [in the next world] would be on the model of this case in [this] world — namely that the double is taken from [the oppressor] but is not returned to its owner, but is rather diverted to other channels. But since, in this world, it was not deemed sufficient of him that he return to the wronged the very thing taken from him, but rather he must hand over to him another the like of it [in addition] — that was an indication that in the world to come this is its case [too]: namely that something of his good deeds is taken from him, and the wronged is thereby compensated (yuʿawwaḍ) in exchange for what was taken from him; and if there be no good deeds there, the compensation (al-ʿiwaḍ) is the lightening of the wronged man's evil deeds and the increase in the wrongdoer's chastisement — just as, when he had not with him in this world the means to make payment, he was enslaved, his servitude being a compensation to the wronged for the wrong done him. And that is confirmed also by [the law of] one who was struck and fell ill: the obligation of his medical treatment, and what is lost to him through his idleness, falls upon the one who struck him — by His saying [Exod 21:19] רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא ("only he shall pay for his loss of time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed"). This, then, is the last of the discourse on reward and punishment.

: The phrase is kāna ʿabdan — literally "he becomes a slave / is enslaved"; rendered "he is enslaved [in payment]," on the model of the biblical sale of the insolvent thief into servitude (Exod 22:2).

: The source's marginal pointer reads Sh-m-y-ʿ d-ʾ, r-p (OCR garble); the citation רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא is Exod 21:19, so the pointer is to be read Shemot, kaf-alef (Exod 21). The merged OCR's קב שבועה for רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ is a consonantal corruption corrected here against the Masoretic text (see diff-report p217).

: Q's own preferred position (alladhī yaṣiḥḥ ʿindanā), set against the transfer-of-deeds view he merely reported in §3. He argues a fortiori from the positive law of restitution: since the Torah obliges a thief/wrongdoer to restore double (ḍiʿf; cf. Exod 22:3/22:6) — and the surplus goes to the victim, not to a third party — eschatological justice must likewise compensate the victim, not merely punish the oppressor into a void. The mechanism is the same merit/demerit transfer of §3, but now derived (not merely reported) and re-grounded in the analogy of the law: restitution-in-kind-plus, enslavement of the insolvent (Exod 22:2), and the assault-victim's medical-and-idleness damages (Exod 21:19) all show that the law's aim is the victim's recompense (ʿiwaḍ). ʿIwaḍ (compensation) is the operative term — the Bahshamī category of deserved recompense (glossary §VI: istiḥqāq); Q's insistence that punishment without restitution would leave the victim uncompensated is a characteristically ʿadl-driven (justice-driven) refinement of the cruder deed-transfer doctrine.
§5 — Close of the anti-Christian section: incidental gains, the deferred refutations, and transition to the ʿĪsāwiyya

We have now given the discourse against the Christians its full due, to the extent that the book admits of that; and what we have said is [but] little of much that lies against them. There have entered into what we mentioned other matters, of the branches of reward and punishment, of [divine] equity (al-taʿdīl) and the imputation of wrong (al-tajwīr), in which the Christians have no part — [matters] whose benefit is not slight. We did that only so that the discourse might be complete.

As for whoever affirmed prophethood (nubuwwa) for עִיסָא (Jesus) — the corruption of his doctrine will be made plain hereafter. And as for whoever, among the Rabbanites (al-Rabbāniyyīn), claimed that עִיסָא worked the miracles (al-muʿjizāt) by way of sorcery (al-siḥr) — we have no need to occupy ourselves with refuting them on that point, since none would say such a thing except one who intends an assault upon prophethood [as such]. For if one who is not a prophet can have come to him what comes to the prophet — the inversion of nature and the [working of] miracles — without prophethood, then there is no security against everyone who claims prophethood and sets up a sign or a miracle [being suspected of] having that sign and that miracle come to him only by the like of that sorcery which עִיסָא worked. And we have already related of them — I mean the Rabbanites — that they allege that they too are able to [do] the like of that, in two ways also: one of them בְּשֵׁם טָמֵא (by an impure name) and the other בְּשֵׁם טָהוֹר (by a pure name). And perhaps we shall relate the doctrine of those who affirm sorcery, and the refutation of them, in another place [than this].
And now we return to the doctrine of the ʿĪsāwiyya (al-ʿĪsūniyya), who are the followers of Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī.

: al-taʿdīl wa-l-tajwīr — the paired technical terms for affirming God's justice (declaring Him just, taʿdīl) versus imputing injustice to Him (tajwīr); a standing Muʿtazilī doublet (cf. al-ʿadl wa-l-tawḥīd).
: The source distinguishes āya (sign) and muʿjiza (miracle/probative miracle); both retained.

: The bab's coda closes the entire anti-Christian block (Babs 1–12) and pivots to the intra-Jewish sectarian polemic of Bab 13 (against Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī's ʿĪsāwiyya). Three loose ends are tied off, each deferred: (1) the digressions on taʿdīl/tajwīr and the "branches of reward and punishment" were included only "so the discourse be complete"; (2) the refutation of those who grant Jesus nubuwwa (prophethood) is promised "hereafter" — i.e., the treatment of false prophecy and the muʿjiza/nubuwwa criteria (glossary §VII), realized in Babs 15–16; (3) the Rabbanite claim that Jesus' miracles were siḥr (sorcery) is dismissed as self-defeating (if non-prophets can work nature-inverting wonders, no prophet's muʿjiza could ever authenticate him) and its full refutation deferred "to another place." The detail that the Rabbanites claim sorcery "by a pure name / by an impure name" (be-shem ṭahor / be-shem ṭameʾ) is a notice of Jewish magical-name praxis (the divine/angelic Names vs. impure names) Q ascribes to his Rabbanite opponents. The closing sentence is the explicit hinge to Bab 13.

- The bab's subject. The heading triangulates three distinct eschatological data: (1) the muwāqafa — the item-by-item arraignment of each person over his deeds, "which some people call al-ḥisāb (the reckoning)"; (2) the mutual beholding — each of the two classes (people of reward, people of punishment) sees the other's lot; and (3) the qiṣāṣ — the exaction of retribution for the wronged from the wrongdoer. The three together complete the reward-and-punishment block (Babs 7–12 of Maqala III, the eschatology staged in glossary §VI) that the closing §5 explicitly seals off before pivoting to the sectarian polemic of Bab 13.

- Arraignment vs. "reckoning." Q's preferred term is muwāqafa (arraignment / confrontation-with-one's-deeds), and the heading pointedly attributes the alternative name ḥisāb ("the reckoning") to "some people" — a distancing that may register either a popular or a Rabbanite/Islamicate idiom Q declines to adopt. Muwāqafa and ḥisāb are both glossary §VI anchor-terms; this bab is their first attestation in the translated M3 corpus.

- The two doctrines of retribution (§§3–4). Q carefully separates a reported view from his own. In §3 he relays — at one remove ("some have said … qiyās would require it") — the bare merit/demerit transfer doctrine: the oppressor's ḥasanāt pass to the victim, or the victim's sayyiʾāt pass to the oppressor. In §4 he gives "what is sound in our view": the same transfer mechanism, but now derived from the positive law of restitution (theft restored double, the insolvent thief enslaved, the assault-victim's medical-and-idleness damages of Exod 21:19) and re-grounded in the principle that justice must compensate the victim (ʿiwaḍ), not merely punish the oppressor into the void. This is the iḥbāṭ/takfīr (merit-cancellation and demerit-expiation) economy of Bahshamī moral theology, refined by Q's victim-centered ʿadl argument.

- The naturalized psychology of §2. The justification of the mutual beholding "by reason" (ʿaqlan) — the soul is "disposed by nature" (maṭbūʿa) to joy at a foe's affliction and grief at a foe's bliss — is a striking instance of Q grounding an eschatological claim in a kalām-style psychological premise rather than in Scripture alone, then reading the prophetic verses (Mic 7:10; Ezek 28:26; Ps 92:12; Prov 24:17-18) as confirming it.

- OCR condition and citation reconstruction. Pages p219–p217 are among the most OCR-degraded in the M3 corpus (the diff-report logs 77 Hebrew disagreements; the Kraken layer is almost entirely corrupt, and the multimodal layer, though far better, fragments the niqqud and drops several marginal pointers). All Hebrew citations have been reconstructed against the Masoretic text from the legible fragments; verse references in brackets follow Q's surviving marginal pointers, corrected silently where garbled. Specific corrections: the opening prooftext כִּי הִנֵּה יוֹצֵר הָרִים is Amos 4:13 (the source pointer is illegible); רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן is Exod 21:19 (OCR קב שבועה corrected; pointer Shemot kaf-alef). One fragment — כְּשֵׂם … שֶׁבֶּן הָאִישׁ הַטּוֹב לִבְּכֶם, preceding the Micah 7:10 citation on p218 — could not be securely identified to a Masoretic verse and is flagged rather than reconstructed (it may be a further sub-citation in the Schadenfreude cluster, or an OCR conflation of two pointers).

- The Psalm-50 courtroom (§1). Q's reading of Psalm 50 as a depiction of the Day of Judgment, with its three classes of defendants summoned in sequence (ḥasidim/righteous, vv. 5–6; the covenant-people / middling, vv. 7ff.; the wicked, v. 16ff.), is the structural spine of the preamble and supplies the graded order in which the resurrected are brought to arraignment.

- For the Bahshamī iḥbāṭ wa-takfīr (merit-cancellation / demerit-expiation) and the transfer-of-deeds economy underlying §§3–4: ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 14 (al-Aṣlaḥ, istiḥqāq al-dhamm, al-tawba) and Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa on al-iḥbāṭ wa-l-takfīr; the doctrine that good and evil deeds can be weighed, cancelled, and transferred is the direct Muʿtazilī parallel. See glossary §VI anchor terms (iḥbāṭ, takfīr, istiḥqāq, ʿiwaḍ, muwāqafa, ḥisāb). - For the eschatological muwāqafa / ḥisāb (arraignment and reckoning) and the rabbinic din we-ḥeshbon parallel: the Rabbanite material Q is implicitly distancing himself from (m. Avot 3:1; b. Ḥagigah; the yom ha-din traditions); for the Karaite eschatological tradition, Daniel Frank, Search Scripture Well (2004), and Haggai Ben-Shammai on Qirqisānī's and Yefet ben ʿEli's Muʿtazilī eschatology. - For the law of restitution underlying §4 (double restitution, sale of the insolvent thief, assault damages): Exod 21:18-19, 22:1-3 — and Q's own legal treatment in the furūʿ (the legal Maqalat of the Anwār, VI–XIII), where the ḍiʿf (double) and shevet/rippui (idleness/healing) damages are adjudicated. - For the sorcery (siḥr) / pure-and-impure-name polemic of §5 and the transition to the ʿĪsāwiyya: Q's Anwār Maqala I account of the Jewish sects (the ʿĪsāwiyya / Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī); Leon Nemoy, "Al-Qirqisānī's Account of the Jewish Sects," HUCA 7 (1930); for the be-shem ṭahor / be-shem ṭameʾ magical-name praxis, the Genizah magical corpus and Steven Wasserstrom on Abū ʿĪsā.
